item.title: Interactive Planar Arm Kinematics & WebAssembly Simulation
item.author: contact@example.org (Smidr Engineer)
item.description:
Robotic manipulators transform actuator joint angles into spatial tool coordinates. In this interactive guide, we analyze the forward kinematics of a two-link planar robotic manipulator using mathematical derivations, vector diagrams, and real-time in-browser code execution.

1. Mathematical Formulation

Consider a two-link planar arm with joint angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and link lengths $l_1, l_2$. The Cartesian coordinates $(x_1, y_1)$ of the elbow joint and $(x_{ee}, y_{ee})$ of the end-effector are governed by trigonometric projection:

$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= l_1 \cos(\theta_1) \ y_1 &= l_1 \sin(\theta_1) \ x_{ee} &= l_1 \cos(\theta_1) + l_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2) \ y_{ee} &= l_1 \sin(\theta_1) + l_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2) \end{aligned}$$

As established by John J. Craig in his foundational robotics treatise [craig2005] , representing these geometric transforms as homogeneous matrices provides computational uniformity for higher degrees of freedom.

2. Kinematic Linkage Diagram (TikZ)

The following schematic is rendered entirely client-side using WebAssembly TeX (TikzJax):

3. Interactive WebAssembly Python Playground

You can modify the joint angles and link lengths in the sandbox below. Click Run (WASM) to compute the end-effector position inside your browser—no backend server computation or cloud latency required!

🔨 Planar Kinematics Solver (Pyodide WASM)
Terminal Output

    

  





4. Including Standalone Source Files


Rather than copy-pasting code into Markdown, Smidr allows referencing clean production scripts directly from your repository using code-file:



    

      

        📄
        kinematics.py
      

      python
    

    
import numpy as np

def forward_kinematics(theta1_deg, theta2_deg, l1=1.0, l2=0.8):
    """
    Computes end-effector (x, y) coordinates for a 2-DOF planar robotic arm.
    :param theta1_deg: Base joint angle in degrees
    :param theta2_deg: Elbow joint angle in degrees
    :param l1: Length of link 1 (meters)
    :param l2: Length of link 2 (meters)
    """
    t1 = np.deg2rad(theta1_deg)
    t2 = np.deg2rad(theta2_deg)
    
    x1 = l1 * np.cos(t1)
    y1 = l1 * np.sin(t1)
    
    x_ee = x1 + l2 * np.cos(t1 + t2)
    y_ee = y1 + l2 * np.sin(t1 + t2)
    
    return (x1, y1), (x_ee, y_ee)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    elbow, ee = forward_kinematics(45.0, 30.0)
    print(f"Elbow Joint Position:  x={elbow[0]:.4f} m, y={elbow[1]:.4f} m")
    print(f"End-Effector Position: x={ee[0]:.4f} m, y={ee[1]:.4f} m")

  



  
💡

  

    
Clean Code Maintenance

    

      By storing algorithms in standalone scripts, your CI test runners can validate your Python code on every commit while your blog renders the exact same file automatically!
    

  





5. Real-Time Parameter Response Tuner


Test closed-loop trajectory tracking response under variable damping ratios and natural frequencies:



  
Robotic Trajectory Response Tuner

  
Adjust velocity gain and damping to observe step response oscillations.


  

    

      

        Proportional Gain ($K_p$):
        2.5
      

      
    


    

      

        Damping Ratio ($\zeta$):
        0.45
      

      
    


    

      

        Natural Frequency ($\omega_n$):
        3.0
      

      
    

  


  






6. Support Open Science & Robotics Research

item.title: Quick Start Guide: Writing & Publishing with Smidr
item.author: contact@example.org (Smidr Engineer)
item.description:
Welcome to Smidr! This guide demonstrates how simple it is to compose and publish rich technical articles using native Markdown and Smidr’s built-in shortcodes.

1. Creating a New Article

To generate a new article with all archetypes and frontmatter preconfigured, simply run:

hugo new posts/my-first-simulation.md

This creates a clean Markdown file in content/posts/ with tags, categories, math mode, and backlink detection already enabled.

2. LaTeX Mathematics

Smidr includes client-side KaTeX for instantaneous rendering of mathematical formulations:

  • Inline equations: Type $f(x) = \sigma(W x + b)$ to render $f(x) = \sigma(W x + b)$.
  • Display equations: Wrap your formula in double dollar signs:

$$\mathcal{L}_{PID}(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau) d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}$$

3. Formatted Code Blocks

Simply write standard markdown code fences. Smidr automatically detects the language, attaches a glowing tag, and provides an animated Copy to Clipboard button:

// Rust kinematics controller loop
pub fn step_controller(target: f64, current: f64) -> f64 {
    let error = target - current;
    let gain = 1.45;
    gain * error
}

Notice that code never line-breaks awkwardly; long lines scroll horizontally without breaking your page layout!

4. Callout Boxes & Admonitions

Highlight crucial observations using the alert shortcode:

💡
Author Tip
You can pick between 5 alert styles: info, warning, caution, tip, and robotics.
🤖
Robotics Hardware Note
Ensure motor current sensors are calibrated before closing the loop on real physical hardware.

5. Client-Side WASM Code Runners

Want your readers to experiment with code right on the page? Embed a Pyodide WebAssembly runner:

🔨 Interactive Python Playground
Terminal Output

    

  





6. Embedded Parameter Sliders


Allow readers to interact with real-time dynamic visualizations:



  
Interactive System Response Tuner

  
Drag sliders to modify system parameters in real time.


  

    

      

        Proportional Gain ($K_p$):
        2.5
      

      
    


    

      

        Damping Ratio ($\zeta$):
        0.45
      

      
    


    

      

        Natural Frequency ($\omega_n$):
        3.0
      

      
    

  


  






7. Secret Text


Hide spoilers, puzzle solutions, or Easter eggs with the secret shortcode:


Here is the secret passcode: CYBER-FORGE-2026


(Hover or select the space above to reveal the payload!)


8. Popover Footnotes


Footnotes in Smidr don’t yank readers away to the bottom of the page1.


9. AI Transparency & Translation Badges


Smidr includes built-in metadata badges for disclosing AI involvement and translation origin. Configure your front matter:


used_ai: true
original_language: "de"
original_post_path: "/de/posts/meine-notizen/"
ai_model: "Ollama / Llama 3"

This renders an automatic provenance banner at the top of the article.


10. OpenPGP Cryptographic Identity Verification


Display your public key, fingerprint, and verification instructions with pgp-card:



  

    

      🔐
      OpenPGP Public Key Verification
    

    RSA 4096 / Ed25519
  


  

    

      

        UID / Identity:
        Smidr Engineer <engineer@example.org>
      

      
      

        Key ID:
        0xA1B2C3D4E5F67890
      

      
      
      
      

        Expires:
        Never
      

      
    


    
    

      
Fingerprint:

      

        ABCD1234EF567890ABCD  1234EF567890ABCD1234
        
      

    

    

    
    

      

        ASCII Armored Public Key
        
      

      

-----BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----
Version: OpenPGP.js v5.1.0

mQGNBGXx... [Your ASCII Armored Key Here] ...
-----END PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----

    

    

    
    

      
        💾
        Download Key (.asc)
      
    

    
  





11. Asciinema Terminal Replay


Embed interactive CLI recordings without external video overhead:


{{< asciinema id="123456" title="Installing PyTorch with CUDA in Conda" >}}

12. Direct File-Based Code Inclusion


Instead of copy-pasting code, reference source files directly from your repository:


{{< code-file source="scripts/train.py" lang="python" title="Training Loop" >}}





    

  1. 

    Hovering or tapping this note opens a popover right here! No losing your reading position. ↩︎
    

    2.

item.title: Interactive Client-Side Code Runners with WebAssembly
item.author: contact@example.org (Smidr Engineer)
item.description:
One of the defining innovations of modern technical blogging is allowing readers to tweak parameters, verify equations, and run algorithms directly on the page.

In this dispatch, we demonstrate how Smidr utilizes WebAssembly (Pyodide) to execute code exclusively in the reader’s local web browser.

💡
Server Security & Resilience Guarantee
Because this static site is hosted on a Raspberry Pi (or GitHub Pages), zero code is ever transmitted to or executed on the server. All Python scripts run in an isolated client-side WebAssembly sandbox. Infinite loops or intensive computations only impact the reader’s local thread and cannot crash or breach the host server.

Live Python Sandbox (Pyodide WASM)

Try running or editing the neural forward-pass below. When you click Run (WASM), the browser lazily loads Pyodide WebAssembly and calculates the activation values on your device:

🔨 Pyodide Forward Pass Sandbox
Terminal Output

    

  





Live JavaScript Evaluation Playground


For fast vector computations, readers can also use the lightweight in-browser JS evaluation sandbox:



  

    

      🔨
      Real-Time Kinematics Vector Calculation
    

    

      
      
      
    

  

  

    

    
    
  

  

    
Terminal Output

    

    

  





Digital Garden Connection


Notice how this post links directly with our previous work on Autonomous Quadrotor Trajectory Optimization with LQR. The bidirectional link detector below discovers and displays this relationship automatically!

item.title: Autonomous Quadrotor Trajectory Optimization with LQR
item.author: contact@example.org (Smidr Engineer)
item.description:
Designing trajectory controllers for autonomous aerial robotics requires balancing agile maneuverability with dynamic stability. As established in foundational optimal estimation theory by Kalman [kalman1960] and classical feedback principles [astrom2010] , we formulate a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) for a 6-DOF multi-rotor system1.

Mathematical Formulation

The linearized continuous-time error dynamics around the hover equilibrium point are expressed via state-space representation:

$$\dot{x}(t) = A x(t) + B u(t)$$

where the state vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$ represents position, velocities, Euler angles, and body angular rates:

$$x = \begin{bmatrix} p_x & p_y & p_z & \dot{p}_x & \dot{p}_y & \dot{p}_z & \phi & \theta & \psi & p & q & r \end{bmatrix}^T$$

The optimal control law minimizes the infinite-horizon quadratic performance index:

$$J = \int_{0}^{\infty} \left( x^T Q x + u^T R u \right) dt$$

The continuous algebraic Riccati equation (CARE) is solved to compute the feedback gain matrix $K$:

$$A^T P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^T P + Q = 0 \implies u(t) = -K x(t) = -R^{-1} B^T P x(t)$$

🤖
Actuator Saturation Warning
Rotational motor velocities are physically bounded by maximum ESC voltage. Saturation $u_{max}$ must be handled with anti-windup clamping to prevent destabilizing non-linear limit cycles.

Control Architecture (Vector TikZ Diagram)

Below is the closed-loop feedback architecture rendered in vectorized SVG directly in your browser using TikZ WebAssembly:

Interactive Control Tuner

You can adjust the damping ratio $\zeta$ and proportional gain $K_p$ in the live system simulator below to observe the pole placement and step response settling time:

Second-Order Closed-Loop Step Response
Drag the sliders below to witness closed-loop damping and transient oscillations in real time.
Proportional Gain ($K_p$): 2.5
Damping Ratio ($\zeta$): 0.45
Natural Frequency ($\omega_n$): 3.0

Secret Telemetry Flag

Here is an encrypted debug marker embedded in this dispatch: KEY-90812-AUTONOMOUS-ROVER-DEPLOYED (Notice how the text above is invisible until you highlight or hover it with your mouse cursor!)

Code Implementation (Python / NumPy)

Below is the state-space feedback loop computation with syntax highlighting, horizontal scrolling, and a copy button:

import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg

def compute_lqr_gain(A: np.ndarray, B: np.ndarray, Q: np.ndarray, R: np.ndarray):
    """Solve Continuous Algebraic Riccati Equation (CARE) and return gain K."""
    P = scipy.linalg.solve_continuous_are(A, B, Q, R)
    K = np.linalg.inv(R) @ (B.T @ P)
    return K, P

# Hover linearized system matrices
A = np.zeros((12, 12))
A[0:3, 3:6] = np.eye(3)
B = np.zeros((12, 4))
B[5, :] = 1.0 / 1.25 # Mass normalized thrust

Q = np.diag([10, 10, 20, 1, 1, 2, 5, 5, 5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1])
R = np.eye(4) * 0.1

K, P = compute_lqr_gain(A, B, Q, R)
print("Optimal LQR Gain Shape:", K.shape)

In our companion article, we expand on WASM Client-side Execution to evaluate neural network controllers directly in the browser!

References & Bibliography

📚 References & Citations

  1. Modern aerial robotics relies heavily on linearized inertial dynamics around hover states before scaling to non-linear MPC. ↩︎
